extracted.intended_audience: students and scholars of philosophy and natural history; educated readers interested in teleology, instinct, and the philosophy of biology
extracted.subtask_description: Exposition and analysis of teleology (final causes) versus efficient causes in nature, and of instinct and mechanical tendencies in animals, with examples and analogies. Aimed at explaining how to recognize and interpret design-like phenomena in organised and unorganised nature.

rubrics_metrics.name: Teleology in organised vs unorganised nature
rubrics_metrics.description: In unorganised nature the final causes withdraw into the background so that explanation by final causes alone is no longer valid and efficient causes are indispensably required; in organised nature teleology is evident and legitimate.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples illustrating the difference include hair distribution and beard as purposive in organised beings, the modified mammary apparatus of cetacea as a teleological adaptation for nursing under water, and plant–insect pollination showing design in organised nature. Note that final causes become ambiguous when dealing with unorganised forces (e.g., why the sea is salt), so one should prefer efficient-cause explanations there.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinction between final causes and efficient causes
rubrics_metrics.description: Final causes (ends, purposes) and efficient causes (mechanisms that bring about appearances) must be distinguished: where the efficient cause is found the final cause may be ambiguous or only appear as an aspect of our point of view.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When the efficient cause becomes visible (e.g., coarse mosaics or the god Apennine at Pratolino only produce effect at a distance), the apparent final cause may vanish. Use the presence or absence of identifiable mechanisms to decide whether to invoke final causes.

rubrics_metrics.name: External design where end lies in another individual
rubrics_metrics.description: A design is 'external' when the end lies in one individual but the means are located in another; such design is more dubious when the assisting individual belongs to a different species or kingdom unless the maintenance of the species depends upon it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Accept external design more readily when the individuals involved belong to the same species (reciprocal adaptation of genitals), or when species maintenance clearly depends on the interaction (many plants that require insects for fructification). Be sceptical of teleological explanations involving unrelated species/kingdoms unless there is clear dependence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reciprocal adaptation as evidence of teleology
rubrics_metrics.description: Reciprocal anatomical and behavioural adaptations (e.g., the complementary organisation of the genitals of two sexes) are strong evidence of teleology in organised nature.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use cases like sexual morphology, the glowworm/lampyris examples (male wings vs female phosphorescence), and plant–insect mutualisms as positive indicators of purposive organisation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid conflating teleology with physico-theology/theism
rubrics_metrics.description: Recognise that teleology (design-like organisation in nature) is not necessarily identical with physico-theology or an argument for speculative theology; many critics reject teleology only because they equate it with theological inference.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Distinguish philosophical teleology from theological claims. Aristotle's approach (finding teleology through unbiased study of nature) is recommended over approaches that immediately turn teleology into evidence for divine providence. Beware of dismissing teleology solely on anti-theological grounds (as Bacon, Spinoza, and others have done).

rubrics_metrics.name: Mechanical tendencies as illustrations of unconscious will
rubrics_metrics.description: Works produced by mechanical tendency (bird's nests, spider webs, ant-lion pits, bee-hives, termite dwellings) show creatures working decisively toward ends which they do not know—evidence that the will can act without conscious representation of the end.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat first-time performances of such structures as paradigmatic: the agent lacks knowledge of the perfected form or use, yet achieves it. These examples support the notion of a will acting blindly toward ends; use them to argue for teleology of organised nature.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition and identification of instinct vs motivation
rubrics_metrics.description: Instinct is a character (an inner tendency) set in motion only by a quite specially determined motive and thus produces actions always of the same kind; motivation (including intellect) acts by giving direction to a broader character and allows variable actions adapted to circumstances.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Identify instincts where an internal, narrowly-determined trigger produces stereotyped behaviour (e.g., migration season, nest-building when pregnant and material present). Identify motivated/intellect-driven actions where an agent adapts to a range of motives and modifies means accordingly (more characteristic of higher animals and humans).

rubrics_metrics.name: Role of intellect in adapting instinctive work
rubrics_metrics.description: Instinct supplies the universal/rule, while intellect supplies the particular/application: animals guided by instinct can still use intellect to direct detail and adapt to circumstances.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Look for evidence of repair and adaptation (spider repairing a destroyed web, bees adapting hive after damage, ants moving larvae when place is too damp). These demonstrate that instinctive constructions are not mere automatism but allow intelligent modification of particulars.

rubrics_metrics.name: Analogy between insect societies and organism (parts subordinated to whole)
rubrics_metrics.description: In insect societies the specialised roles of individuals (queen laying eggs, workers cultivating young, drones impregnating) parallel organs of an organism; each part's life is subordinated to the life of the whole, sometimes involving sacrifice of individuals for the collective.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use examples such as ants creating a dam of dead bodies, workers stinging drones to death when useless, two queens fighting, and caste-specific behaviours to illustrate organism-like teleology at the level of societies. This analogy supports interpreting collective structures teleologically.

rubrics_metrics.name: Healing and reparative processes as analogues to instinctive problem-solving
rubrics_metrics.description: The organism's healing power (closing wounds, compensating for lost functions) is analogous to how insects repair or modify their works when obstacles occur; both show the will's capacity to meet disturbances ingeniously.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cite examples like tissue regeneration, neural/vascular compensations, and insect behaviours such as repairing webs or the burying-beetles undermining a stick to sink a tied frog. Use such analogies to argue for purposive, adaptive processes rather than purely mechanical outcomes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Anticipation of future needs in instinctive behaviour
rubrics_metrics.description: Instinctive actions often anticipate future needs that the animal does not yet feel, including care for future broods and pre-emptive defence (e.g., Bombex pursuing and killing enemies of future eggs).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognise forward-looking features in instinct as evidence of teleological organisation: animals act for ends not presently experienced, which supports interpreting their behaviour as purposive even without conscious foresight.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ambiguity and anti-patterns that challenge teleological explanations
rubrics_metrics.description: There are ateleological instances and anomalous facts (e.g., the unsuitableness of sea-water for drinking) which can be cited to derange teleological conceptions and show that final-cause explanations can be misapplied.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When evaluating alleged design, consider counterexamples and paradoxes; these may indicate that appeal to final causes is inappropriate or that efficient-cause explanations are needed. Use such anti-patterns to test the limits of teleological interpretation.
